title: Faith and the state
hook: Sikhs hold different views on religion and politics; the Gurus spoke truth to rulers

segments.voice: Yesterday, the portrait of the Khalsa: pure, brave, disciplined, generous. Your line was khalsa means pure. What did you do with a single, clean motive? Day one thousand four hundred eleven.

Kings are tigers, and their officials are dogs. That isn't a protest sign. It's a line of scripture, in a salok of Guru Nanak, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib. It says out loud, about the powerful, what the people under them might only whisper at home. The village clerk, the tax collector, the guard at the gate: the ones who knock at night. Guru Nanak doesn't flatter them, and he doesn't flatter the throne behind them either. Today: faith and the state, and the Gurus who spoke truth to rulers.
screen: `KINGS ARE TIGERS.` → `A LINE OF SCRIPTURE.` → `TRUTH TO RULERS.`

segments.voice: First, Guru Nanak's words. In the salok, in paraphrase: kings are tigers, their officials are dogs; they go and wake the sleeping to harass them. The servants of power wound people with their claws. That's blunt language about rulers, with no single king named. A few weeks ago, this path heard the Babarvani, his hymns on an invasion, which call the invading host a wedding party of sin. The salok turns the same honesty on ordinary rule. Second, the throne facing the temple. Tradition says Guru Hargobind wore two swords, miri and piri, worldly authority and spiritual authority, and built the Akal Takht, the Throne of the Timeless One, facing the Harmandir Sahib. The message Sikhs draw from it: faith has something to say to power, and doesn't bow to it. Third, honest disagreement. Sikhs today hold different views on how faith and politics should meet. Some see miri-piri as a call to stay engaged in public life, as Sikhs, together. Others keep faith out of party politics and put it into service and conscience instead. Both draw on the same Gurus, and the tradition holds room for both. Fourth, what they share. Speaking truth to rulers isn't the same as wanting to rule. The Gurus' words name injustice plainly, without flattery and without hatred. Truth to rulers can be as large as a hymn about an invasion, or as small as one honest sentence at a city council, in an office, at a family table where one person's word is law.
screen: `KINGS ARE TIGERS.` · `MIRI AND PIRI, TWO SWORDS.` · `SIKHS DISAGREE, HONESTLY.` · `NAMING INJUSTICE, NOT RULING.` · then, large: `TRUTH TO RULERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak one honest word. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a place where power sits over you: a boss, an office, a rule, an institution, even a family elder. Is there one honest thing that needs saying there and hasn't been said? Don't draft a speech. Find the one sentence. Turn it over, breath by breath, until it's both true and kind. Then picture saying it, steadily, without flattery and without cruelty. If you pray, you can ask for courage in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Faith and the state. Sikhs hold different views on how they meet, and the Gurus, from the Babarvani to the Akal Takht, spoke truth to rulers. Today's word.
Your line: truth to rulers. Today, say one honest word to someone with power over something, clearly and kindly, even if it's only a well-written email. Day one thousand four hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's hymns and saloks on rulers, including the Babarvani, as part of the Guru Granth Sahib and look to the Akal Takht in Amritsar as a seat of temporal authority; Sikhs differ on how directly faith should engage in politics.
